neighbours.label: the foundations of computing as a subject: the halting problem, Turing machines, computability and early codebreaking, peaking on the key noun ('problem' in 'the halting problem', 'machine' in 'a Turing machine'); the same nouns in everyday senses (a washing machine, a problem set) and the Turing test stay low
fire: No program can decide, for every input, whether another program halts: that is the halting problem.
In 1936 Turing described an abstract machine that manipulates symbols on an infinite tape.
Any function a Turing machine can compute is called computable.
Church and Turing showed that the decision problem cannot be solved in general.
A universal Turing machine can simulate any other Turing machine.
The proof that the halting problem is undecidable uses a diagonal argument.
At Bletchley Park the bombe machines helped break Enigma traffic.
Busy beaver numbers grow faster than any computable function.
quiet: No plumber can decide, for every house, whether an old pipe leaks: that is the real problem.
In 1936 the factory installed a sewing machine that stitched cloth on a long table.
Any recipe a home cook can follow is called easy.
The city council showed that the parking problem cannot be solved quickly.
A universal remote can control any other television.
The proof that the bridge is safe uses a load test.
At the fair the slot machines took most of our coins.
Ticket prices grow faster than any wage.
